title: Love is the fruit
hookLine: Narada brags, gets a monkey's face, and his sutras say love is the fruit
carry: bhakti is the fruit, and God loves humility
last: DROP THE FRUIT, NOT THE WORK.

cards: You may remember the sage Narada from year one. He sat so deep in meditation that Kama, the god of desire, couldn't move him, and Narada was thrilled with himself. He bragged to Shiva, then to Vishnu.

Then, in a city Vishnu conjured, he fell for a princess and begged Vishnu for his handsome face so she'd choose him. He walked into her hall with the face of a monkey. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it.
Tradition credits that same Narada with a short book on love, the Narada Bhakti Sutras. Today it makes its boldest claim, with a reason the monkey-faced Narada would understand.

teach.b: In paraphrase: bhakti, the sutras say, is greater even than karma, jnana and yoga: action, knowledge and the disciplined stilling of the mind. Why? Because it is of the form of the fruit.
Phala-rupa. The fruit is what the tree is for. So the sutras aren't calling the other roads worthless.
They're saying love is what those roads walk toward: work done as an offering, knowing that clears the mind, a mind held still, all finding their point in love. Then a second reason.
The Lord, the sutras say, dislikes pride and is fond of humility. The Sanskrit for that humility is dainya: lowliness, the state of someone with empty hands.

Narada had beaten desire and turned the win into a trophy, and the princess's hall took it from him. In the sutras' picture, love has a hard time doing that, because it keeps looking at the beloved, not at itself.
That's the heart of bhakti, the path of loving devotion that runs through so much Hindu worship: the bhajan, the lamp, the flower offered with folded hands are meant as gifts, not performances.
That's this text's view; other Hindu teachers weigh the roads differently.
Shankara's school, which we met in year two, holds that knowledge is what frees, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Both are living Hindu paths.
Tomorrow the sutras ask, out loud, whether knowledge is the means to love.

how: In devotional Hindu communities, the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied in short sections with a teacher, and lines like these on love as the fruit and the Lord's fondness for humility are explained with stories of devotees.

o: devotion: love that is the fruit, not only the road
a ritual that earns merit for the next life
knowledge of God gained from long study

games.q: love as the fruit — tap the pairs.
p: of the form of the fruit

s: the sutras call karma, jnana and yoga worthless
they call bhakti greater, because it is the fruit those roads are walking toward.
the sutras say the Lord dislikes pride and is fond of humility
that is their second reason for placing love highest.
every Hindu school agrees that love stands above knowledge
that is Narada's view. Shankara's school holds that knowledge frees, with devotion readying the mind.

games.q: you've spent years on a discipline, and you're good at it. the sutras say love is greater. how do they explain that?
o: your discipline was a waste of time.
love is the fruit the roads are for, and the Lord loves humility.
love is easier, so it wins.
games.why: the sutras give two reasons: bhakti is of the form of the fruit, and the Lord dislikes pride and is fond of humility. nothing is said to be wasted.

practice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and notice anything you're holding up like a trophy today: something you did well, something you know, how long you've practiced.

Don't scold it; set it down beside you the way you'd put down a bag, and rest with the hands open. If you pray, you can turn toward God with those open hands; if not, simply stay with what it's like to hold nothing up.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. In the Narada Bhakti Sutras, not only a road but the fruit itself, and close to humility, dainya, the open hand.

orig.note: Sanskrit dainya, humility, lowliness: the sutras say the Lord is fond of it and dislikes pride.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti is the fruit, and God loves humility. Offer it as a gift, not a trophy. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 25–27 (bhakti greater than karma, jnana and yoga; because it is the fruit; because the Lord dislikes pride and loves humility)
